title: Building a chicken coop from pallets
subtitle: A step-by-step guide to a low-cost pallet-framed coop for a small laying flock.
excerpt: A pallet-framed chicken coop can be built over a weekend with basic tools and reclaimed timber. The structure uses standard EUR pallets as wall frames, lined with exterior-grade ply for weatherproofing, with a felted or corrugated roof. It is suitable for four to six hens as a starter coop and uses materials that cost little or nothing when pallets are sourced from local businesses.
sourceNotes: DEFRA Code of Recommendations for the Welfare of Laying Hens (2018), space requirements. British Henkeepers Association, Hen Housing Standards (2022). Various online pallet coop builds, adapted for UK climate and welfare standards.

glossaryTerms.definition: The small opening in a chicken coop through which hens enter and leave. It should be closable at night against predators and sited on the sheltered side of the coop.

A standardised European pallet measuring 1,200 mm by 800 mm, made from softwood with a load-bearing capacity of around 1,500 kg. The most common type available from supermarkets, builders' merchants, and industrial premises.

projectSchedule.title: Sourcing materials
projectSchedule.body: Source pallets, timber, screws, mesh, and roofing felt. Allow a weekend day for collecting materials and checking pallets for damage.

projectSchedule.title: Build day one: frame and walls
projectSchedule.body: Stand pallets, secure wall frames, add exterior plywood cladding. Cut pop-hole opening. Fit door frame.

projectSchedule.title: Build day two: roof and fittings
projectSchedule.body: Fit roof frame and felt or corrugated sheet. Install perches, nesting boxes, ventilation. Paint with exterior wood treatment.

projectSchedule.title: Introduce hens
projectSchedule.body: After paint or treatment has fully cured and dried (check the product label). Introduce hens at dusk to encourage roosting in the new coop on the first night.

content.text: A pallet coop uses
EUR pallets

as the structural skeleton of the walls, lined with plywood or OSB to make them weatherproof. The pallets provide framing for free; the cost goes on screws, cladding, mesh, roofing felt, and fixings. A basic coop for four to six hens comes together over two days with standard hand tools.
Selecting and siting

Pallets sourced free from supermarkets or DIY merchants should be stamped "HT" (heat treated), not "MB" (methyl bromide fumigated). Heat-treated pallets are safe for use with animals; methyl-bromide pallets are not.
Plan for at least 0.4 m squared of floor space per bird, plus nesting boxes and perch space. Four hens need a coop of at least 1.6 m squared of floor.
Site the coop on level, well-drained ground. Raise it on bricks or low concrete blocks to stop the pallet bases rotting from ground moisture.
Materials for a four-to-six-hen coop
Four EUR pallets for the walls (two 1,200 mm pallets for front and back; two 800 mm pallets for the sides).
Two sheets of 9 mm exterior-grade plywood or OSB for cladding.
Roof batten and corrugated polycarbonate or roofing felt for the roof.
50 mm wood screws, joist hangers or angle brackets for joining pallets.
19 mm welded wire mesh for ventilation openings.
Two or three 50 mm diameter round perch poles and nesting box material.
Day one: building the frame
Stand the back pallet vertically and use angle brackets at the base to fix it to a batten screwed to the ground frame or base board. Angle brackets every 600 mm at the base are sufficient.
Attach the two side pallets at right angles to the back pallet using joist hangers or timber brackets screwed through the pallet frames.
Fit the front pallet, leaving a gap for the door. A standard pallet with a section removed at one end makes a simple door frame.
Clad the outside of the walls with exterior ply or OSB, screwing into the pallet frame boards. Overlap the cladding at corners to cover the joint.
Cut the
pop-hole
in the lower part of one wall: 250 mm wide by 300 mm high for standard breeds. Frame the opening with a batten surround to stop the edges of the ply splitting.
Day two: roof and interior fittings
Build the roof frame from softwood battering, sloped toward the back or side for water run-off. Fix to the top of the pallet walls.
Cover with roofing felt, lapped upslope and nailed with clout nails. Or use corrugated polycarbonate on timber purlins for a lighter roof with more light inside.
Fit ventilation: a 100 mm gap under the ridge covered with 19 mm welded mesh, or two round vents in the top of the gable ends.
Install perches at around 600 mm height, 300 mm from the wall and from each other. Allow 200 mm of perch per bird.
Fit one nesting box per three hens, positioned darker and lower than the perches. A simple 300 mm cube with a lowered front sill and a hinged lid for egg collection works well.

attrs.cue: Pallets are difficult to join squarely at the corners
attrs.cause: Pallets vary slightly in dimension and squareness
attrs.fix: Clamp pallets together, check diagonal measurements are equal, then screw. A few mm of variance at the corner joint does not matter once the cladding is on.

attrs.cue: Coop feels damp inside after first rain
attrs.cause: Roofing felt insufficiently lapped, or cladding boards have gaps
attrs.fix: Check the felt lap: each strip should overlap the one below by at least 75 mm. Apply a bead of exterior sealant at any visible gaps in the cladding joints.
